1. In a block, 45 of 60 sampled children are fully immunised. Test against a target of 85%. Check the Normal-approximation condition first, then give z and the two-sided p-value.

Condition: np₀ = 60 × 0.85 = 51 and n(1 − p₀) = 60 × 0.15 = 9, both ≥ 5, so the Normal approximation is acceptable (a convention, §5.7.2.2.4). p̂ = 45/60 = 0.75. SE under H₀ = √(0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 60) = √0.002125 = 0.0461. z = (0.75 − 0.85) ÷ 0.0461 = −2.17. Two-sided p = 2 × P(Z < −2.17) = 0.030. At α = 0.05, coverage is below the 85% target. If the 60 children came from a few villages, the SE should allow for clustering (§6.2.6).

2. ORS use during the last diarrhoea episode was 60/100 in Block A and 45/100 in Block B. Compute the two-proportion z statistic, then the Pearson χ² from the expected counts, and show that χ² = z².

p̂_A = 0.60, p̂_B = 0.45, difference 0.15. Pooled p̄ = 105/200 = 0.525. SE₀ = √[0.525 × 0.475 × (1/100 + 1/100)] = √0.0049875 = 0.0706. z = 0.15 ÷ 0.0706 = 2.12 (p = 0.034). Expected counts: users 100 × 105/200 = 52.5 in each block; non-users 47.5 in each block. Every |O − E| = 7.5. χ² = 7.5² × (1/52.5 + 1/47.5 + 1/52.5 + 1/47.5) = 56.25 × 0.0802 = 4.51. z² = 2.124² = 4.51 = χ².

3. Why does the one-proportion test use p₀ in the SE while the confidence interval uses p̂?

A test calculates how surprising the data would be if H₀ were true, so every part of the calculation, including the SE, assumes p = p₀. A confidence interval makes no assumption about the true value; it estimates the SE from the data, using p̂.

1. Explain why a paired t-test is generally more powerful than an independent samples t-test for detecting the same size of change.

Each person’s difference removes their stable level (their “baseline” BP or haemoglobin). The SD of the differences, s_d, therefore excludes between-person variation and is usually much smaller than the SD of either measurement. A smaller SE gives a larger t for the same mean change. The independent test leaves the between-person variation in the SE.

2. Group 1: n = 12, mean SBP 128 mmHg, SD 10. Group 2: n = 15, mean 120 mmHg, SD 18. Compute the pooled t (with df) and the Welch t (with Welch–Satterthwaite df). Which SE is larger here, and why?

Pooled: s_p² = (11 × 100 + 14 × 324) ÷ 25 = (1,100 + 4,536) ÷ 25 = 225.4; s_p = 15.01. SE = 15.01 × √(1/12 + 1/15) = 15.01 × 0.3873 = 5.82. t = 8 ÷ 5.82 = 1.38, df = 25 (p = 0.18). Welch: v₁ = 100/12 = 8.33, v₂ = 324/15 = 21.6. SE = √29.93 = 5.47. t = 8 ÷ 5.47 = 1.46. df = 29.93² ÷ (8.33²/11 + 21.6²/14) = 896.0 ÷ (6.31 + 33.33) = 22.6 (p = 0.16). The pooled SE is larger. Pooling weights each variance by its df, so the larger group’s larger variance (324) dominates s_p², and that inflated value is then applied to the smaller group as well. Here the pooled test is conservative. When the smaller group has the larger variance, the pooled SE is too small and the pooled test gives too many false positives. Welch avoids both.

3. Sixteen children have mean haemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, s = 1.6 g/dL. Test against a hypothesised value of 12 g/dL (t₁₅, 97.5% point = 2.131). State t and your conclusion.

SE = 1.6 ÷ √16 = 0.4. t = (11.2 − 12) ÷ 0.4 = −2.00, df = 15. |t| < 2.131, so do not reject H₀ at α = 0.05 (p = 0.064). The 95% CI, 11.2 ± 2.131 × 0.4 = 10.35 to 12.05 g/dL, includes 12 but also values well below it: the study is inconclusive, not evidence that the mean is 12.

4. Nine pregnant women have haemoglobin measured before and after a month of supervised IFA. The mean change (after − before) is 0.45 g/dL with s_d = 0.60 g/dL. Compute the paired t, its df and the 95% CI (t₈, 97.5% point = 2.306), and state your conclusion.

SE = s_d ÷ √n = 0.60 ÷ √9 = 0.20 g/dL. t = 0.45 ÷ 0.20 = 2.25, df = 9 − 1 = 8. |t| < 2.306, so do not reject H₀ at α = 0.05 (p = 0.055). 95% CI: 0.45 ± 2.306 × 0.20 = 0.45 ± 0.46 = −0.01 to 0.91 g/dL. The data are compatible with no change but also with a rise of nearly 1 g/dL: nine women are too few to settle it, which is not the same as showing IFA has no effect.

1. A dataset fails the Shapiro–Wilk test with n = 2,000. Should you conclude it is unfit for a parametric test? What should you look at instead?

No. With n = 2,000 the test detects departures too small to matter, and the Central Limit Theorem makes the sampling distribution of the mean close to Normal even for moderately non-Normal data. Look at a Q-Q plot (and a histogram) to see the kind and size of the departure, and at skewness. Only marked skew or extreme outliers would call for a transformation or a non-parametric method.

2. A right-skewed variable, household income, is log-transformed before a t-test. The mean log income is 0.18 higher in village X than in village Y, with 95% CI 0.02 to 0.34. What does the difference represent on the original scale? Give the point estimate and CI.

A t-test gives a difference, not a coefficient. The difference of mean logs is the log of the ratio of geometric means. Back-transform: e^0.18 = 1.20, so the geometric mean income in village X is about 20% higher than in village Y. 95% CI: e^0.02 = 1.02 to e^0.34 = 1.40. It cannot be read in rupees, because it is a ratio, and it says nothing directly about the arithmetic means.

1. A one-way ANOVA comparing four clinics is significant. A colleague concludes “all four clinics differ from each other”. What is wrong, and what should be done next?

A significant F says only that the four means are not all equal: at least one differs from at least one other. It could be one clinic differing from the other three. To find which pairs differ, use a multiple comparison procedure: Tukey’s HSD for all six pairs, or Dunnett’s test if each clinic is compared with one reference clinic. Report the pairwise differences with their adjusted CIs. (These procedures do not require the F-test to be significant first.)

2. A study tests 8 independent hypotheses at α = 0.05, all nulls true. What is the FWER? What is the Bonferroni per-test α?

FWER = 1 − 0.95⁸ = 1 − 0.663 = 0.337: about a one-in-three chance of at least one false positive. Bonferroni per-test α = 0.05 ÷ 8 = 0.00625.

3. A one-way ANOVA has 4 groups and N = 24, with SSB = 6.0 and SSW = 20.0. Complete the ANOVA table and decide at α = 0.05 (the 95% point of F(3, 20) is 3.10).

Source SS df MS F
Between 6.0 4 − 1 = 3 2.0 2.0
Within 20.0 24 − 4 = 20 1.0
Total 26.0 23

F = 2.0 < 3.10: do not reject H₀ (p = 0.15). The data do not show a difference between the group means; they do not show the means are equal.

1. Using the table in §9.5.4, compute the supplementation gain at clinic A and at clinic B, and the difference between the two gains. What does a non-zero difference of this kind represent?

Gain at A = 2.85 − 2.80 = 0.05 kg. Gain at B = 3.30 − 2.85 = 0.45 kg. Difference of gains = 0.45 − 0.05 = 0.40 kg. A difference between the effect of one factor at different levels of the other is an interaction: the benefit of supplementation depends on the clinic. Neither main effect can show this, because each averages over the other factor.

2. Haemoglobin is measured in 40 pregnant women at 0, 2 and 4 months; 9 miss the 4-month visit. What does RM-ANOVA do with those 9 women, and name two better approaches.

RM-ANOVA needs complete data, so it drops the 9 women entirely, including their 0- and 2-month values. That loses 22.5% of the sample (9 of 40) and can bias the result if the women who missed the visit differ (for example, sicker or poorer). Better: (a) a summary-measure approach, such as each woman’s change per month computed from the visits she attended, analysed with a one-sample or two-sample t-test (Matthews et al., 1990); (b) a linear mixed model (§15.2.4), which uses every available measurement and allows unequal timing.

3. Four children’s weights gain 0.20, 0.30, 0.10 and 0.20 kg per month. Using the summary-measure approach, compute the mean gain and its SE.

Mean = 0.80 ÷ 4 = 0.20 kg/month. Deviations 0, 0.10, −0.10, 0; SD = √(0.02 ÷ 3) = 0.0816 kg/month. SE = 0.0816 ÷ √4 = 0.041 kg/month. (A one-sample t-test against 0 would give t = 4.9 on 3 df.)
